### 26.12 The Threads That Run Through Your Whole Resume

If an interviewer asks *"What's your architecture philosophy?"*, these patterns appear in almost every role. Each one has proof from at least two places on your resume:

| Principle | Where it shows up |
|---|---|
| **Find the common model, turn N × M into N + M** | TRDDC (common IR), DCP (canonical data model, config-driven templates), ADP (shared reference architecture) |
| **Put slow or unreliable work behind a queue** | DCP (Kafka), VoxAlchemy (Redis queue + worker), PlantGuard (governed tool calls) |
| **Make everything safe to retry (idempotency)** | DCP consumers, LLM calls, Garnishment deductions, PlantGuard purchase orders, Delta MERGE |
| **Variation belongs in data, not code** | DCP templates and rules, Garnishment effective-dated rules, metadata-driven ETL framework |
| **Classify work by what it can tolerate, then optimize each class** | Spot vs on-demand, SLA-tagged pipelines, confidence routing, PlantGuard auto vs human review |
| **The model isn't the product; the system around it is** | LLM extraction (85% → trustworthy), PlantGuard (guards, judge, evals), VoxAlchemy (quality scores) |
| **Fix the pattern, not the instance** | 500-job template fix, paved roads at ADP, consumer pattern adopted platform-wide |
| **Measure it or you can't claim it** | SLOs and p95, sampling audits, golden-set evals, cost per job and per document |

**One line to end on:** *"Across 22 years the technology changed from static analysis to microservices to agents, but the architecture moves stayed the same: find the common model, isolate the unreliable parts, make everything safe to retry, and measure what you promise."*



### 26.13 DCP as a multi-tenant SaaS: each sector is a tenant

**The story in one line:** one DCP platform serves several financial sectors (USPF, Corporate, Governance, SF and others). Each sector is a tenant with its own data, rules, users and limits. The code and the infrastructure are shared.

⚠ *The repo names USPF, Corporate and Governance. "SF" is taken from your notes, probably Structured Finance. Replace this list with your real sectors before you use it.*

#### Why a sector is the right tenant

Sectors differ in almost everything that matters to the business: source channels, document templates, taxonomy, validation rules, approval chains, dissemination targets, regulatory audit needs, and who is allowed to see the data. A tenant is exactly that kind of boundary.

The 50 asset classes and the 4 business lines are not separate tenants. They become **configuration and roles inside a tenant**. That keeps the number of tenants small (about five) and makes each one a real business boundary. ⚠ Check whether your 4 business lines map onto your 5 sectors. If they do, say so; it simplifies the story.

#### Shared platform vs per tenant

| Shared (platform) | Per tenant (sector) |
|---|---|
| Kafka, extraction services, workflow engine, rules engine code | Templates and extraction schemas ([§26.7](#267-automated-template-onboarding-across-1000-templates-24-days--under-1-hour)) |
| Kubernetes, CI/CD, observability, AI model gateway | Taxonomy mappings to the internal model |
| The UI code | Validation rules and confidence thresholds (>0.9 / 0.7–0.9 / <0.7) |
| Security controls and the tenant-aware APIs | Dissemination targets and schedules |
| | Users, roles and approval chains (L1, L2) |
| | Data: documents, extraction results, events |
| | Audit trail, encryption key, quotas (documents per day) |

#### How one document flows through the tenant

1. **Tenant is set at the door.** A document arrives through its sector's source (an S3 bucket, an email inbox, Delta Sharing). The sourcing service maps that source to a tenant ID. The tenant is never guessed later.
2. **Tenant travels with every event.** Kafka messages carry the tenant ID in their headers. The key is `tenantId + documentId`, so ordering holds per document, and sectors share partitions fairly.
3. **Extraction loads the tenant's settings.** The worker uses that sector's template, schema and model configuration.
4. **Routing uses the tenant's thresholds.** Auto-approve, L2 review or manual extraction follows that sector's rules.
5. **Access is scoped.** Approvers see only their own sector's documents. Every query is filtered by tenant.
6. **Dissemination goes to that sector's targets only.**

#### Isolation choices

- **Data:** one PostgreSQL schema per sector. The DCP deployment plan already says "isolate data per tenant (different PostgreSQL schemas)." MongoDB and Elasticsearch use a `tenantId` on every document or index, with a tenant filter on every query. Governance data can get its own database if its regulator requires it. ⚠ Confirm what was built, versus what was planned.
- **Access:** the tenant is a claim in the access token ([§29](#29-oauth-20-and-jwt-service-to-api-story)). Each service checks it against the resource being requested, not just against the login.
- **Keys:** one encryption key per sector, so one sector's data can be deleted or cut off without touching the others.

#### Fairness and limits

A quarter-end filing burst in one sector must not delay another sector's SLA. The same bulkhead idea as [§26.1](#a-availability-99-no-single-failure-takes-the-platform-down), applied per tenant:

- Quotas per sector: documents per day and concurrent extractions.
- Separate processing lanes or Kafka consumer groups for SLA-critical sectors.
- Latency and throughput dashboards per tenant, so a noisy neighbour shows up before a customer complains.

#### Adding a new sector

A new sector is **configuration, not code**: create the tenant, load its templates (AI-drafted and human-reviewed, as in [§26.7](#267-automated-template-onboarding-across-1000-templates-24-days--under-1-hour)), set its rules and thresholds, create its users and roles, and set its quotas. This is what makes onboarding scale.

#### Releases per tenant

Shared code means one bug can reach every sector at once. Roll out changes one tenant at a time: a feature flag per tenant, then a canary on one sector, then the rest. A rollback can also be applied to one tenant only.

#### 60-second answer

> "DCP is a multi-tenant platform. Each financial sector is a tenant: USPF, Corporate, Governance, SF and the others. The code and infrastructure are shared, so one release serves every sector. What belongs to a sector is everything that describes its business: templates, taxonomy, validation thresholds, dissemination targets, users, quotas, audit trail and encryption key. The tenant is set when a document enters through its source, and it travels in the Kafka key and headers, so ordering holds per document and no event crosses sectors. Isolation is a schema per sector in PostgreSQL, a tenant filter on every query, and a key per sector. For fairness, each sector has quotas and its own processing lanes, so a quarter-end burst in one sector doesn't break another's SLA. A new sector is configuration, not code."

#### Likely follow-ups

- **"How do you stop data leaking between sectors?"** The tenant is set once, at ingestion. Every query is filtered by it. Access is checked against the token's tenant claim. Cross-tenant tests run in CI, and every access is audited.
- **"Why not one database per sector?"** For a handful of tenants, that multiplies cost and operations. Use stronger isolation only where a regulator requires it.
- **"How do you release a change to one sector first?"** A feature flag per tenant, then a canary on that sector, with rollback applied to that tenant only.
- **"Can a sector use a different AI model?"** Yes. Model choice is per-tenant configuration behind the LLM gateway ([§26.6](#266-multi-modal-llm-extraction-pipeline-2-analyst-days--20-minutes-979-faster-presidents-award)).

#### ⚠ Confirm before using

- The full list of sectors, and what SF stands for.
- Whether your 4 business lines map onto your 5 sectors.
- Whether the production schema was per sector, or whether it stayed a planned design.
- Per-sector numbers and quotas.

### 26.14 How a tenant reaches the database: UI to DB in DCP

**The story in one line:** one common UI serves every sector. The user signs in once, picks the sector when they ingest a document, and the server checks that choice before the document is stored in that sector's schema.

#### The steps

**1. Login is common.** Every user signs in once through Okta, with the same UI for all sectors. The token doesn't name one tenant. It lists the tenants the user belongs to:

```json
{
  "sub": "user-42",
  "tenants": ["uspf", "corp"],
  "scp": ["documents:write", "documents:read"],
  "aud": "api://dcp",
  "exp": 1760003600
}
```

Okta builds the `tenants` list from group memberships, such as `uspf-ingest` and `corp-ingest`.

**2. The user picks the sector at ingestion.** The UI shows only the sectors in the token's list. The user chooses "USPF" and uploads a file. The UI sends the choice with the request:

```
POST /documents
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{ "tenant": "uspf", "fileName": "filing-2026-10.pdf" }
```

**3. The API checks the choice.** The UI's choice is treated as a request, not a fact. The server checks:

- Is `uspf` in the token's `tenants` list? If not, the answer is `403`, whatever the UI sent.
- Does the token allow `documents:write`? If not, `403`.

**4. The service picks the schema.** Once the check passes, the service maps the tenant to its schema through a whitelist, sets the request's tenant context, and switches the database connection to that schema, as described in [§26.13](#2613-dcp-as-a-multi-tenant-saas-each-sector-is-a-tenant). The document is written to `uspf.document`.

**5. The tenant is fixed for the document.** The tenant is stored with the document and never chosen again. Later reads, approvals and exports use the document's own tenant, not the user's current selection. A user who switches sectors in the UI doesn't move documents between sectors.

**6. Storage and events carry the tenant.** The file is stored under a tenant prefix, for example `uspf/<documentId>.pdf`. The Kafka event carries the tenant in its key and headers, so downstream processing uses that sector's rules and schema.

```
UI (common, one login)
  │  token: tenants = [uspf, corp]
  │  user picks "USPF" at ingestion
  ▼
API gateway ──> Ingestion service
                  1. "uspf" in token tenants? no → 403
                  2. documents:write scope?   no → 403
                  3. tenant → schema (whitelist) = uspf
                  4. SET search_path TO uspf; INSERT document
                  5. store file under uspf/…, publish Kafka event (key: uspf + documentId)
```

#### Reads and approvals

Every later request checks the user's access against the document's tenant. A user who is in USPF but not in CORP can't see a CORP document, even if they open it by ID. The check is "is this user in the document's tenant?", not "which tenant is selected in the UI?"

#### Optional: a tenant-scoped token

For stricter control, the API can exchange the common token for a token limited to the chosen sector (token exchange, RFC 8693). Downstream services then see only `tenant: uspf`. Use it where the stricter boundary is needed, since it adds one more token exchange per request.

#### Pitfalls

- **Trusting the UI's choice.** The check against the token is always on the server.
- **Letting the selection change a document's tenant.** The tenant is set once, at ingestion.
- **Missing checks on reads.** Opening a document by ID must be checked against its tenant too.
- **Stale context in background jobs.** Kafka consumers set the tenant from the message and clear it afterwards, as in [§26.13](#2613-dcp-as-a-multi-tenant-saas-each-sector-is-a-tenant).

#### 60-second answer

> "The UI is common to all sectors. The user signs in once, and the token lists the sectors they belong to. At ingestion, the user picks a sector, and the UI sends that choice with the upload. The server checks the choice against the token and the user's write permission, then maps the sector to its schema and writes the document there. The sector is stored with the document, so every later read and approval checks the document's own tenant. The file and the Kafka event carry the tenant too, so downstream processing uses that sector's rules and schema."

### 26.15 DCP on AWS: the full footprint, native vs managed, spot, secrets and uploads

The full content now sits in [§18, DCP on AWS](#dcp-on-aws-footprint-native-vs-managed-spot-secrets-and-uploads), next to the AWS interview material. This section stays in §26 so the resume story keeps its link.

### 26.16 How to reach 99%, 99.9% and 99.999% availability

**The simple version:** availability is the share of time a system works. Each extra "nine" cuts the allowed downtime by about ten times, and costs much more to achieve. DCP's 99%+ came from removing single points of failure, separating slow work from user-facing work, and making releases safe.

#### 1. What each level allows

| Availability | Downtime per year | Downtime per month | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| 99% (two nines) | about 3.6 days | about 7.3 hours | Internal tools, batch systems |
| 99.5% | about 1.8 days | about 3.6 hours | DCP's requirement target |
| 99.9% (three nines) | about 8.8 hours | about 44 minutes | Most business SaaS |
| 99.95% | about 4.4 hours | about 22 minutes | Enterprise SaaS with SLAs |
| 99.99% (four nines) | about 53 minutes | about 4.4 minutes | Payments, core banking |
| 99.999% (five nines) | about 5 minutes | about 26 seconds | Telecom, emergency systems |

#### 2. The idea behind every level

Availability fails in four ways. Each level of nines removes more of them:

1. **A part breaks.** A server, disk or zone dies. *Fix:* spare copies of everything.
2. **Nobody notices quickly.** The system is down but no one knows. *Fix:* health checks and alerts, so detection takes seconds.
3. **The fix is slow.** Failover is manual or untested. *Fix:* automatic failover, and rehearsed runbooks.
4. **We break it ourselves.** Releases and config changes cause outages. *Fix:* small, reversible releases.

The last one causes many real outages, so it deserves as much attention as hardware.

💡 **MEMORY TRICK: "FDFC"**

Four ways a system goes down, and four matching fixes:

```
F = Fail      (a part breaks)            → spare copies of everything
D = Detect    (nobody notices quickly)   → health checks and alerts
F = Failover  (the fix is slow or manual) → automatic failover, rehearsed
C = Change    (we break it ourselves)    → small, reversible releases
```

Say it as: "Fail, detect, fail over, change." Each extra nine is about making all four faster and safer.

#### 3. What it takes, level by level

**99% to 99.5%: basic redundancy**
- Two or more copies of each stateless service.
- Regular backups, and a restore that has been tested.
- Health checks that restart a broken process.

**99.9%: no single point of failure**
- Every component is spread across at least two availability zones.
- The database has a standby that takes over automatically.
- Timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers on every remote call.
- A message queue between slow work and user-facing work, so a slow dependency becomes lag, not an outage.

**99.95%: safe change**
- Canary releases, with automatic rollback when error rates rise.
- Pre-flight checks before each deploy, and expand-then-contract database changes.
- On-call rotation, runbooks, and blameless postmortems.

**99.99%: survive a whole region**
- Two or more regions. Active-passive is the usual start: a standby region takes over.
- Automated, rehearsed failover, with data replicated across regions.
- Chaos testing: deliberately break things in production-like environments to prove the failover works.
- Bulkheads: one slow dependency can't use up the threads or connections that other features need.
- Graceful degradation: when a feature fails, the rest keeps working.

**99.999%: no planned downtime, and no weak dependency**
- Active-active regions: every region serves traffic all the time.
- Cell-based design: the system is split into isolated cells, so a failure hits one cell, not all users.
- Zero-downtime upgrades for every component, including the database.
- Every dependency must meet the same target. A 99.9% vendor caps the whole system at 99.9%.
- Very high cost in engineering, operations and money. Few systems justify it.

#### 4. Why it multiplies down

If a user request must pass through three services, each at 99.9%, the chain is available about 99.7% of the time (0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999). Each extra step in a synchronous chain lowers availability. This is why asynchronous queues and fallbacks matter for high targets.

#### 5. How DCP reached 99%+

- **No single point of failure:** stateless services with multiple replicas, multi-zone deployment, and standby databases.
- **Slow work behind a queue:** AI extraction runs asynchronously through Kafka. A vendor outage becomes a delay, not downtime ([§26.1](#261-delivered-99-availability-and-95-accuracy-under-2s-latency-processing-10k-documentsday-dcp)).
- **Fallbacks:** circuit breakers, plus a second extraction engine when the first one fails ([§27.10](#2710-designing-retries-for-a-failing-downstream-without-a-retry-storm)).
- **Safe change:** canary releases, pre-flight checks and fast rollback. This is what cut incidents from 60 to 24 a month ([§26.3](#263-cut-production-incidents-60-and-mttr-6-by-re-architecting-legacy-monoliths-into-event-driven-microservices)).
- **Fast recovery:** MTTR went from 2 hours to 20 minutes. At 99% or better, how quickly you recover matters as much as how rarely you fail.

**To go beyond 99.9%** you would also need multi-region failover, which the DCP design planned but did not run as active-active. Say so honestly if asked.

#### 6. Interview answer

> "Availability is the share of time a system works. 99.9% allows about 44 minutes of downtime a month. To reach 99%+ in DCP, I removed single points of failure, spread every component across zones, and put the slow AI work behind Kafka with fallbacks, so a vendor outage meant delay, not downtime. Releases were canary-based with automatic rollback, and recovery time dropped from 2 hours to 20 minutes. Going to 99.99% needs multi-region failover, and 99.999% needs active-active regions and zero-downtime upgrades everywhere, at a much higher cost."

#### 7. Likely follow-ups

- **"What's the difference between availability and reliability?"** Availability is whether the system responds now. Reliability is whether it responds correctly over time.
- **"Why not just add more servers?"** Servers don't help if the database, a zone or a bad release takes everything down. Redundancy must cover every layer.
- **"How do you measure it?"** Success rate from the user's point of view, measured at the gateway or by synthetic checks, over a rolling 30 days. Uptime from a server's own view can look better than what users see.
- **"Does a planned maintenance window count?"** Usually yes, if the SLA says so. That is why zero-downtime upgrades matter at the top levels.

⚠ *Confirm the exact DCP measurement method and the number you will quote. The requirement was 99.5% and the resume says 99%+.*

## 27. Java Scenario Q&A

**What this is:** 15 short production scenarios from senior Java and architect interviews. Each answer gives the first thing to check, then the fix. Where this guide already covers the idea in depth, there's a link.

### 27.1 Spring Boot API suddenly takes 5–6 seconds in production

Don't guess. Find the slow hop first.

- Check the endpoint's latency metric (Micrometer and Actuator) to confirm it's this endpoint, not everything.
- Open a trace (OpenTelemetry with Jaeger or Zipkin). The longest span is the suspect: a database query, an outbound HTTP call, or your own code.
- Take 2–3 thread dumps (`jcmd <pid> Thread.print`), a few seconds apart. Threads stuck in the same place point to the bottleneck.
- Check HikariCP metrics. Many pending connections means the pool is the problem, not the query.

Fix the hop you found, then confirm with the same metric.

### 27.2 HashMap works in tests but breaks under concurrent access

`HashMap` is not thread-safe. Two threads calling `put` at the same time can overwrite each other's entries, lose data, or leave the internal table inconsistent, and readers can see partial results. Old Java (7 and earlier) could even loop forever during a resize.

Tests pass because they usually use one thread, which never triggers the race. Iterating while another thread changes the map can also throw `ConcurrentModificationException`.

Fix: use `ConcurrentHashMap` for shared data, with atomic methods like `merge` and `computeIfAbsent`. Wrap access in `synchronized` only when you need several steps to stay consistent together.

### 27.3 200 threads, but throughput is still low

Threads that are waiting don't add work. Take a thread dump and count threads by state.

- Many `BLOCKED` threads on the same lock: a `synchronized` block around shared work.
- Many `WAITING` threads for a database connection: the pool is too small for 200 threads.
- Many threads blocked on one slow downstream call.
- CPU-heavy work on far more threads than cores: the CPU spends its time switching between threads.

Throughput is roughly concurrency ÷ latency (Little's Law). To go faster, either reduce the time each request takes or remove the resource that limits concurrency. Fix the bottleneck, not the thread count.

### 27.4 OutOfMemoryError after running for hours

Read the message first:
- `Java heap space`: objects are piling up in the heap.
- `Metaspace`: too many classes loaded, often a classloader leak on redeploy.
- `unable to create native thread`: too many threads, not too much heap.

For a heap problem, start the JVM with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` to capture the state at the moment of failure. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT and read the "Leak Suspects" report, which shows what holds the memory.

Check GC logs too. If memory after each full GC keeps climbing, it's a leak. Common causes: a static or unbounded cache with no eviction, listeners that are never removed, `ThreadLocal` values not cleared in a thread pool, or an unbounded queue in an executor.

### 27.5 Two requests update the same row at the same time

This is a lost update: both read the same balance, both write, and one change disappears. Three options:

- **Optimistic locking (usual default):** add a `version` column (JPA `@Version`). An update that finds a different version fails, and you retry. Works well when conflicts are rare.
- **Pessimistic locking:** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (JPA `@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)`) locks the row until the transaction ends. Use it when conflicts are frequent and retries would be costly.
- **One atomic statement:** `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?`, then check the row count. Simplest when the change is a single arithmetic update.

### 27.6 One of three downstream services is slow and drags the whole API down

A slow dependency is worse than a dead one, because its callers' threads stay blocked. Protect each downstream:

- **Timeouts:** every outbound call has one, so no thread waits forever.
- **Bulkhead:** a separate thread or connection pool per downstream, so the slow one can only use its own share.
- **Circuit breaker (Resilience4j):** after repeated failures, stop calling it for a while and fail fast.
- **Fallback:** return cached, default or partial data when the optional part fails.
- Call independent services in parallel with `CompletableFuture`, each with its own timeout, so one slow call doesn't hold up the others.

### 27.7 Kafka consumer lag keeps growing, but the consumers look healthy

"Healthy" means running, not keeping up. Check in this order:

- **Rates:** is the producer faster than the consumer? Look at processing time per record.
- **Partition count:** consumers beyond the number of partitions sit idle, so partitions cap parallelism.
- **Slow work inside the consumer:** a database or HTTP call for every message.
- **Hot partition:** one key sends most of the traffic. Lag sits on one partition while the rest are fine.
- **Rebalancing:** if a batch takes longer than `max.poll.interval.ms`, the consumer is removed from the group and the group keeps rebalancing. Lower `max.poll.records` or raise the interval.

To see lag per partition, run `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group <group>`.

### 27.8 A client retries after a timeout and creates duplicate data

Make the operation idempotent, so a repeat does no harm:

- The client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header: one UUID per business operation, reused on every retry.
- The server stores the key with its result, in the same transaction as the write. A repeat with the same key returns the stored response instead of writing again.
- Add a unique constraint on the business key as a safety net, so two concurrent duplicates fail at the database.
- Expire old keys after a set period, such as 24 hours.

The check and the write must be atomic, which is why the key and the data go in one transaction. The messaging version of the same idea is [idempotent consumers](#idempotent-consumers-vs-the-outbox-solving-double-processing).

### 27.9 Database CPU hits 100% right after a deployment

Start with what the release changed:

1. **Top queries by total time:** `pg_stat_statements` (PostgreSQL), Performance Insights, or the slow-query log. Compare with the numbers from before the deploy.
2. **Query plans:** run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the new or slowest queries. A missing index, or a switch to a full table scan, is the most common cause.
3. **ORM patterns:** an N+1 query (one query per row in a loop), or a relation that now loads far more rows.
4. **Connection count:** a pool change can flood the database with connections.

If you find a clear regression, roll back first to stop the damage. Then fix the query and redeploy.

### 27.10 Designing retries for a failing downstream without a retry storm

A retry storm happens when every caller retries at once, adding load to a service that's already struggling. To avoid it:

- **Few retries:** 2–3 attempts, never unlimited.
- **Exponential backoff with jitter:** wait about 1s, 2s, 4s, with random spread so clients don't retry in sync.
- **Retry only transient failures** (timeouts, 503, 429 with `Retry-After`), and only on idempotent operations. Never retry a 400 or a 404.
- **Circuit breaker:** stop retrying altogether while the downstream is down.
- **Retry at one layer only.** Retries at the gateway, the service and the client multiply: 3 × 3 × 3 is 27 attempts for one click.

### 27.11 High GC activity, but traffic is low

Low traffic with heavy GC usually means memory is being held, not churned.

- **Memory leak:** after each full GC, the old generation stays high and keeps growing. Confirm with GC logs (`-Xlog:gc*`) and a class histogram (`jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram`). See [GC - Garbage Collection](#gc---garbage-collection).
- **Large objects per request:** reading a whole file or a big JSON into memory, even at low traffic.
- **A scheduled job** loading a large dataset.
- **Heap sized wrongly for the container:** in Docker or Kubernetes, size the heap against the container's memory limit (for example `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`). A heap that is too small causes constant GC.

Find the memory cause before you tune GC settings.

### 27.12 Two services must update data together, with no distributed transaction

Use a **saga**: a sequence of local transactions, one per service, where each step has a **compensating action** that undoes it if a later step fails.

Example: the Order service creates an order, Payment charges the card, and Inventory reserves stock. If the stock reservation fails, the payment is refunded and the order is cancelled.

To make it reliable:

- Each step writes its state change and its event in one local transaction, using the [transactional outbox](#transactional-outbox-pattern). An event is never lost, and never sent without its change.
- Each consumer is idempotent, because events can be delivered more than once.
- Pick **orchestration** (one coordinator tracks the steps, easier to debug) or **choreography** (services react to each other's events, looser coupling, harder to follow).

### 27.13 Works with 10 users, unstable at 1,000 concurrent requests

Load doesn't slow the system down evenly. It hits a limit, and queues grow fast. The approach:

1. **Reproduce it with a load test** (k6, Gatling or JMeter), using realistic data and think time. Increase the load in steps.
2. **Watch the saturation signals:** CPU, heap, thread count, connection pool usage, database CPU, p99 latency and error rate.
3. **Find the first resource that saturates.** That's the bottleneck. It's often a connection pool, a thread pool or one lock. Also look for missing timeouts, where requests pile up with no end.
4. **Fix it, then re-test** to find the next bottleneck.

Little's Law explains the cliff: as utilization nears 100%, waiting time rises sharply.

### 27.14 Is production latency coming from Java code, the database, the network or an external service?

Measure each hop instead of guessing:

- **Distributed tracing** (OpenTelemetry with Jaeger or Zipkin) shows each span: the inbound request, each DB query, each outbound call. The largest span is the first suspect.
- **Connection pool wait** (HikariCP metrics): time spent waiting for a connection is a pool-sizing problem, not a database problem.
- **Database time:** the slow-query log or `pg_stat_statements` shows query time on the database side.
- **External call time:** client-side metrics for each outbound call, with its timeout and status code.
- **Java code time:** if the spans are short but the request is still slow, use a profiler (Java Flight Recorder or async-profiler) to see where the CPU goes, and thread dumps to see blocked threads.
- **Network:** compare caller and callee timings, and check DNS and TLS setup time in client metrics.

Add up the spans. The biggest share is where to look.

### 27.15 The microservices have become a distributed monolith

A distributed monolith has the costs of microservices and the coupling of a monolith. Signs:

- Services must be deployed together.
- Services share a database or a schema.
- Long synchronous chains: A calls B, B calls C, C calls D, so one failure breaks the whole chain.
- One feature change touches several services at once.

To detect it, map the call graph from your traces, and measure how often one change spans several services.

To prevent it:

- **Database per service:** each service owns its data and shares it only through APIs or events.
- **Async events** for work that doesn't need an immediate answer.
- **Short sync chains:** one or two hops at most.
- **Contract tests** (consumer-driven, for example Pact), so a service can change without breaking its callers.
- **Bounded contexts:** draw service boundaries around business capabilities, not technical layers. See [microservices pitfalls](#16-microservices-when-pitfalls-culture-patterns).

The test: can each service be deployed alone, on any day, without coordinating with other teams? If not, it's still a monolith.

## 28. WFS Senior Solution Architect (ADP) Q&A

**Role:** Senior Solution Architect, G4 L2, Global Product and Technology. The JD is for the WorkForce Software (WFS) platform: a multi-tenant SaaS for workforce management on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Modules include Time & Attendance, Absence, Job Scheduling, Fatigue Management, EmpLive rostering, Analytics, mobile time, and clock integrations.

**What the JD really tests:** three things. (1) Can you design a **multi-tenant, configuration-driven** platform where payroll-grade correctness holds? (2) Can you **govern integrations** (REST, Kafka, gRPC, SOAP, files) so many systems can change safely? (3) Can you **lead architecture** across product, SRE, security and delivery without direct authority? Every answer below is built around one of these.

**How to use this section:** each answer gives the design first, then the honest position on your experience. Where it links to another part of this guide, the earlier section has the full story. Items marked ⚠ need your confirmation before you use them.

### 28.A Fit and gaps (read this first)

#### Q0. JD requirement vs your evidence

### 28.B Role and leadership

#### Q1. How do you lead architecture across product, enterprise architecture, UX, SRE and security when you don't manage them?

Influence through written decisions. Use an **architecture decision record (ADR)** for each significant choice: the context, the options, the trade-off, and the owner. Hold a short design review with the leads who will be affected, and bring data (cost, latency, risk) rather than preference. Put a review date on every decision, so a choice can be revisited when the facts change. Escalate only when a decision is stuck and the cost of delay is known. Authority comes from being the person who makes the trade-offs clear.

#### Q2. What would you do in your first 90 days on WFS?

Map the **operational loop** end to end: HR and identity import, employee and assignment context, time capture from timesheets, clocks and schedules, policy-driven calculation, exceptions and balances, approvals, and export to payroll, finance and analytics. For each step, note the owner, the volume, the SLO and the most frequent incident. Read six months of production incidents and customer escalations: they show where the architecture is actually weak. Then pick one or two problems to fix, not ten.

#### Q3. What do you standardize across modules, and what do you leave alone?

Standardize what must be identical everywhere: tenant context, API versioning, the error model, idempotency keys, trace IDs, the event envelope, and security controls. Leave domain logic to each module. The rule: if a mistake would affect every tenant or break an integration, standardize it. Otherwise, let the module decide. This keeps the platform consistent without turning the architecture group into a bottleneck ([ProductSquads Q19](ProductSquads-JD-Expected-Questions.md#q19-how-do-you-establish-architecture-governance-without-becoming-a-bottleneck-in-a-fast-moving-team)).

### 28.C Multi-tenant SaaS on OCI

#### Q4. Compare tenant isolation models. Which would you choose for WFS?

Three models:

1. **Shared schema, `tenant_id` on every row.** Cheapest and easiest to operate. The risk is a missing filter leaking data. Enforce it in a tenant-scoped data access layer and with database row-level security. On Oracle, that is **VPD** (Virtual Private Database). On PostgreSQL, it is row-level security (RLS).
2. **Schema per tenant.** Stronger separation, but migrations must run across hundreds of schemas.
3. **Database per tenant.** Strongest isolation and protection from noisy neighbours, but the highest cost.

For a platform with many mid-size customers, I'd choose **shared schema with row-level security**, and move the largest or regulated tenants to a dedicated schema or database. That hybrid is common because it keeps most tenants cheap and gives the big ones isolation they can justify. In DCP, this is the sector-as-tenant model: [§26.13](#2613-dcp-as-a-multi-tenant-saas-each-sector-is-a-tenant).

#### Q5. How do you stop one tenant's load from slowing down the others?

Apply limits per tenant at the gateway (requests per second) and in the workers (concurrent jobs). Give large tenants their own queues or Kafka partitions. Use priority for payroll-critical work so a bulk analytics job cannot delay an export. Track latency and throughput **per tenant**, so you see a noisy neighbour before the customer calls. This is the same bulkhead idea as [§26.1](#a-availability-99-no-single-failure-takes-the-platform-down), applied per tenant. The DCP version of this is per-sector quotas and lanes: [§26.13](#2613-dcp-as-a-multi-tenant-saas-each-sector-is-a-tenant).

#### Q6. What does OCI change in the design, and how would you ramp up?

The design rules are cloud-neutral. OCI maps onto what you already know:

- Compartments for isolation by environment or tenant tier (similar to AWS accounts).
- OCI IAM policies with least privilege (similar to AWS IAM).
- Private subnets with controlled ingress (similar to a VPC).
- OKE for managed Kubernetes.
- Object Storage for files (similar to S3).
- Data Guard for database failover and DR.

⚠ Verify each service name and its current feature set against Oracle's documentation before you use the list in an interview.

#### Q7. Design disaster recovery for WFS with different targets per module.

Tier the modules by business impact. Time capture and payroll export are the most critical: target **RPO near zero** and **RTO under one hour**, using synchronous or near-synchronous database replication (Data Guard). Analytics can tolerate **RPO of 24 hours**. For the architecture: an active-passive setup across regions, object storage replicated across regions, Kafka topics mirrored or rebuilt from source with idempotent replay, a documented DNS failover runbook, and a DR drill every quarter. Synchronous cross-region replication adds latency, so choose it per tier, not for everything. See [multi-region vs multi-AZ](#multi-region-vs-multi-az-why-the-jump-is-harder-than-it-looks).

#### Q8. How do you handle the 7 a.m. clock-in spike?

Clock traffic is bursty: hundreds of thousands of punches arrive within minutes of a shift starting. Design for the peak, not the average:

- Terminals and mobile apps buffer punches locally and retry on network loss.
- The ingestion API accepts the punch quickly (202 Accepted) and processes it asynchronously through Kafka.
- Autoscale the workers on consumer lag, not CPU.
- Rate-limit per terminal, so one faulty clock cannot flood the system.
- Make punch ingestion **idempotent**: use device ID plus punch timestamp plus sequence number as the key, so a retried punch never creates a duplicate.

Load-test the peak with a margin of two to three times. The same design logic is in [§26.1 (throughput)](#c-throughput-10kday-headroom-to-20k-scale-out-never-up).

### 28.D Policy-driven calculation and assignment-scoped processing

*This is the core of the JD. Practise it until it is second nature.*

#### Q9. How do you design configuration-driven policy evaluation?

Treat rules as **data, not code**. Policies (rounding, overtime, breaks, absence accrual) are versioned records with an effective date, a scope (tenant, policy profile, assignment), and a defined evaluation order. The engine is generic and **deterministic**: the same inputs and the same policy version always give the same result. Test each policy profile with golden cases, the same way DCP tests templates with golden documents before publishing. Store the policy version used for every calculated result, so you can explain any number later.

#### Q10. What does "assignment-scoped processing" mean, and why does it matter?

An employee can hold several assignments at once: different jobs, locations or pay rules. Each assignment can follow a different policy profile. So processing must be scoped to the **assignment**, not the employee. Punches, schedules and rules are evaluated per assignment, and results are keyed by assignment ID and period. Partition the work by tenant plus assignment, so it parallelizes safely and a recalculation touches only the affected assignments. The mistake to avoid is calculating at employee level and applying the wrong policy to the second job. ⚠ Confirm WFS's exact assignment model.

#### Q11. A policy changes retroactively. How do you recalculate safely?

Effective-dated policies make the change well defined. Find the affected assignments and periods, recalculate only those, and compute the **delta** against the previously published result. Show the delta for approval before it reaches payroll. The recalculation must be idempotent and re-runnable, and it should write **new result versions** rather than overwrite, so the audit trail keeps both old and new values. Once a period is exported to payroll, lock it and make corrections as adjustments in a later period. ⚠ Confirm WFS's current practice for locked periods.

#### Q12. How do you model balances, such as accruals and usage?

Use an **append-only ledger**. Every accrual, usage and adjustment is an entry with an ID, a date, an assignment, the policy version and the source event. The balance is the sum, or a periodic snapshot kept for speed. Append-only gives you auditability, and a recalculation becomes "reverse and re-post" rather than an edit. Give each entry an idempotency key, so a retried job cannot accrue the same hours twice. This is the event-sourcing idea behind DCP's audit trail ([§3](#3-distributed-systems--large-scale-compute-design)).

#### Q13. How do you make a payroll export correct, not just fast?

Treat the export as a contract with strict validation:

1. Write the records to a **staging** table first.
2. Validate each record (format, mandatory fields, ranges).
3. **Reconcile control totals** against the calculation: record count, sum of hours, sum of amounts.
4. **Quarantine** bad records with a reason, rather than silently dropping them.
5. Publish only when reconciliation passes, and keep a signed-off report for each run.
6. Give each export batch an ID, so a re-run is idempotent and cannot pay twice.

Control totals are the real safeguard. A missing employee is a payroll error, and only a reconciliation catches it.

### 28.E Integrations and API contracts

#### Q14. How do you govern contracts across REST, SOAP, gRPC and files?

One standard per protocol: **OpenAPI** for REST, **WSDL/XSD** for SOAP, **protobuf** for gRPC, and a documented schema for files. Versioning rule: only additive changes inside a major version. A breaking change needs a new version and a deprecation window. Run **consumer-driven contract tests** in CI, so a provider cannot ship a change that breaks a consumer. Enforce the standards with a linter and an architecture review checklist. I've done the REST and Kafka side in production; the governance rules are the same for SOAP and gRPC, and I'd ramp up on their tooling.

#### Q15. How do you import employee data from HR and identity systems reliably?

Most HR feeds arrive as batch files or JDBC pulls. Design:

- **Staging, then validation, then upsert.** Never write raw rows straight to production tables.
- **Delta detection:** process only changed records.
- **Idempotent upsert** keyed on source employee ID plus effective date, so a re-sent file changes nothing.
- **Quarantine** bad rows and send the client a report.
- **Provisioning and SSO** (SCIM) so logins and roles follow the HR record.
- **Ordering:** the assignment must exist before time capture arrives. For late-arriving data, use a reprocessing path, not rejection.

#### Q16. What is your standard for idempotency, errors and retries across integrations?

Every write endpoint and every consumer accepts an **idempotency key**. Errors use one model, **RFC 9457 problem details** (`application/problem+json`). Retries apply only to transient errors, with exponential backoff and jitter. Poison messages go to a **dead-letter queue** with the failure reason. Every message and call carries the **trace ID** and **tenant ID**. The full mechanics are in [§27.8](#278-a-client-retries-after-a-timeout-and-creates-duplicate-data) and [§27.10](#2710-designing-retries-for-a-failing-downstream-without-a-retry-storm).

#### Q17. How would you design Kafka topics for many tenants?

Two options. **One topic per event type**, with tenant ID in the key, is the common choice: many tenants share the partitions, and ordering holds per key. **One topic per tenant** gives strong isolation but creates a topic explosion across hundreds of tenants. I'd use shared topics keyed by tenant plus assignment, enforce per-tenant quotas, and give the largest or most regulated tenants their own topics. The partition key determines the ordering guarantee, so choose it from the ordering need ([Kafka partition key](Java-And-MyProfessional-Projects-Interviews/Kafka-Questions.md#8-how-should-dcp-choose-a-partition-key)). In DCP, the tenant is the sector, and it is part of the Kafka key: [§26.13](#2613-dcp-as-a-multi-tenant-saas-each-sector-is-a-tenant).

#### Q18. How do you manage schema evolution for events?

Use a schema registry with Avro or Protobuf and a compatibility rule, usually **BACKWARD** or **FULL**. Add new fields as optional with defaults. Never rename a field or reuse a field number. Deprecate before you remove. Consumers ignore unknown fields. In CI, test both old and new consumers against the new producer. The schema ID travels with each message, so a consumer always knows how to read it.

#### Q19. Flink, Kafka consumers or batch: when do you use each?

Be honest: I haven't run Flink in production. The distinction is still clear:

- **Kafka consumer services** for per-event business logic with transactions.
- **Stream processing** (Flink, or Kafka Streams or Spark Structured Streaming) for stateful work: windows, joins across streams, rolling aggregates. Example: a live alert when a shift goes over its overtime threshold.
- **Batch** for period-end calculation and large reprocessing.

Key point: stream results are **provisional** until the period closes. The payroll figure must come from the calculation engine, never from a live stream aggregate.

### 28.F Security and identity

#### Q20. Walk through an OAuth2/OIDC login. Where does CAS fit?

The user signs in with the identity provider. OIDC returns an **ID token** (who the user is) and an **access token** (what they can call). For a web app, use the authorization code flow with PKCE. APIs validate the **JWT** locally: signature (using the provider's published keys), issuer, audience and expiry. Services call each other with client credentials, or with mTLS. CAS is a central SSO protocol that uses tickets rather than tokens, and it is common in enterprise systems. The architecture is the same: one central login, and each application validates the credential. ⚠ Confirm WFS's exact CAS setup before you describe it.

#### Q21. What is RBAC vs ABAC in a workforce product? Give an example.

RBAC gives coarse permissions: "an approver can approve timesheets." ABAC adds attributes: "an approver can approve timesheets only for employees in their own org unit, in an open period, and never their own." Practical design: use RBAC for the broad roles, then check attributes (tenant, org unit, assignment scope) in the service layer or a policy engine. Log every decision for audit. **Self-approval** is a classic compliance failure, so test it explicitly.

#### Q22. How do you protect employee PII and keep an audit trail?

- Encrypt in transit (TLS 1.2 or higher) and at rest.
- Mask or tokenize sensitive fields (national IDs, bank details), and restrict reads by role.
- Keep keys in a managed vault (OCI Vault, or AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault on other clouds), and rotate them.
- Record an audit entry for every read or change of sensitive data: who, when, which tenant, and before and after values, in append-only storage.
- Never log PII.

The security baseline is in [NFR.md (Security)](Java-And-MyProfessional-Projects-Interviews/NFR.md#security).

### 28.G Data and Oracle

#### Q23. Design the time punch table for volume and retention.

Punches are high-volume, append-only time-series data:

- **Partition by month** (range partitioning), so old data can be archived without scanning the table.
- **Index** on (tenant, assignment, punch time), matching the calculation's access pattern.
- **Never update in place.** A correction is a new row that points to the original.
- **Retention:** archive old partitions to cheaper storage according to the policy for each tenant.
- Bulk-load on ingestion where possible.

On Oracle: range partitioning with local indexes. On PostgreSQL: declarative partitioning. ⚠ Confirm WFS's actual schema.

#### Q24. A query is slow in production. How do you troubleshoot it on Oracle or any RDBMS?

Start with the top SQL by elapsed time: AWR and ASH reports on Oracle, or `pg_stat_statements` on PostgreSQL. Check the execution plan for full scans, a bad join order or a missing index. Check for stale optimizer statistics, and for lock waits. Fix with an index or a query rewrite, refresh the statistics, then re-run and compare the numbers. Same method as [§27.9](#279-database-cpu-hits-100-right-after-a-deployment).

### 28.H Operations, Java and architecture practice

#### Q25. The payroll export is missing 40 employees. How do you investigate?

Start from the control totals and find the stage where records disappear: input, calculated, validated, exported. Trace by batch ID across services using the trace ID. Check the quarantine table for rejected records and their reasons. Check recent changes to assignments or policy profiles, especially their effective dates. Fix the cause, reprocess the batch idempotently, and add a control check that would have caught the problem earlier. Write it up as a root-cause analysis with a clear remediation, the same way as [the 60% incident reduction](#cutting-production-incidents-60-explained-simply).

#### Q26. Tomcat or embedded Spring Boot? What are your 12-factor rules for services?

Spring Boot with an embedded server is the default for new services: each one is self-contained, stateless, containerized, configured from its environment, logs to stdout, and starts and stops quickly. That's the 12-factor model. Keep an application server such as Tomcat only for legacy WARs during a migration, and move them out with the strangler pattern. This is the same shift I led at ADP ([§26.8](#268-adp-application-architect-10-years-microservices-and-containerization-shift-hcm-and-garnishment-platforms-200-engineer-community)). ⚠ Confirm the Tomcat experience you can name.

#### Q27. How do you apply DDD and SOLID to a workforce domain?

Use **aggregates** with clear boundaries. The **Timesheet** (or period) aggregate owns its entries and approval state. **Assignment** holds a reference to its policy profile. **Policy** is its own bounded context, with versioned rules that the calculation consumes. Use the language of the business: assignment, punch, accrual, exception. For SOLID: one responsibility per rule type, new rule types added through a **Strategy** rather than an if-chain, and integration ports (HR, payroll) behind **Adapters**. Keep invariants inside the aggregate, for example "a manager cannot approve their own timesheet", so they can't be bypassed. See [design patterns](design_patterns.md).

### 28.I AI, AIDLC and modern delivery

#### Q28. Where would you use AI and agents in WFS, and where would you not?

**Use them for:** explaining exceptions to managers in plain language, answering policy questions over policy documents with retrieval and citations, drafting correction requests, and triaging operational alerts for SRE.

**Do not use them to calculate** pay, hours or balances. Those must be deterministic and auditable. Agents act only through **governed tools** (APIs that enforce RBAC), and anything that changes pay needs human approval. This is the same design as PlantGuard: deterministic code for facts, LLMs for reading and explaining, and human gates for risky actions ([§26.10](#2610-plantguard-iit-hyderabad-capstone-multi-agent-predictive-maintenance-copilot)).

#### Q29. What does AIDLC mean to you, and how would you use it?

⚠ Confirm the meaning WFS uses. My working definition is an AI-driven development lifecycle: AI helps with requirements, design drafts, test generation, code review and documentation. Humans own the decisions and the merges, and golden tests guard the behaviour. The adoption approach is the same as my earlier answers ([ProductSquads Q1–Q3](ProductSquads-JD-Expected-Questions.md#1-ai-native-engineering--coding-agent-adoption-high-priority) and [§25.6](#256-ai-first-sdlc-inside-engineering)).

### 28.J Localization, accessibility and time zones

#### Q30. How do localization and accessibility affect the architecture?

Localization is more than translation:

- Store UI text as keys, not hard-coded strings.
- Store timestamps in UTC, and convert to the employee's time zone at display.
- Handle currency and number formats per locale.
- Support right-to-left layouts where needed.

**Time zones are an architecture issue, not a UI issue.** A punch at 11:30 p.m. local time may fall on the next day in UTC. If the day boundary is calculated in the wrong zone, the hours land on the wrong day. Define the business day in the employee's local time zone and store that rule with the policy.

Accessibility means WCAG-compliant UI, keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, and an accessible design system. Automate checks in CI (for example with axe). I haven't led frontend accessibility work in depth, so I'd name a strong frontend lead for it, as in [ProductSquads Q14](ProductSquads-JD-Expected-Questions.md#q14-the-role-mentions-reacttypescript-nodejs-rest-apis-microservices-your-background-is-stronger-in-javapythonspring-boot-how-would-you-lead-teams-in-technologies-outside-your-deep-expertise).

### 28.L Quick reference: 60-second answer for the architecture question

> "For WFS I'd start by mapping the operational loop, from HR import and time capture through policy calculation, approvals and payroll export, and finding where it's weakest. Architecturally, three things matter most. First, a **shared-schema, row-level-secured** tenant model, with the largest tenants isolated when needed. Second, **policies as versioned, effective-dated data**, so every calculation is deterministic, explainable and recomputable, scoped to the assignment. Third, **contract-governed integrations** with idempotent writes, staged validation and reconciled payroll exports. Around that: DR tiered by module, an append-only ledger for balances, and clear rules for where AI helps and where it must never touch pay. I haven't run OCI or Flink in production, and I'd ramp up on those first, but the design principles carry over directly."

## 29. OAuth 2.0 and JWT: Service-to-API Story

**What this is:** one end-to-end story, told simply, of how a service gets permission to call another service. It's the client credentials flow, so no person is involved. It covers keys, JWTs and the checks the receiving API runs. The user-login side of OAuth (redirects, PKCE, ID tokens) is separate and is covered in [§28 Q20](#q20-walk-through-an-oauth2oidc-login-where-does-cas-fit).

**What is OAuth, and what is not in this story:** OAuth 2.0 is the rulebook for getting permission. JWT is the format of the token. Public and private key signing is how the token is protected. This story uses all three. The user-login parts (redirect, PKCE, ID token) belong to OpenID Connect and are not in this story.

### 29.A The story: the Report API asks the Billing API for prices

The **Report API** needs the price list from the **Billing API**. No person is involved. The Report API proves who it is with a **key**, not a password. **Okta** checks that proof and issues a pass, called an access token.

**Step 0: Setup (done once).**
An admin registers the **Report API** in **Okta** as a service application. There are two key pairs in the story:
- The **Report API** creates its own key pair. It keeps the **private key** locked in a secrets manager and gives the **public key** to Okta.
- **Okta** has its own signing key pair. Its private key signs every pass. Its public key is published on Okta's key list, so anyone can check passes.

Okta gives the Report API a **client ID**, its public name. The admin grants the app the `read:billing` scope. The **Billing API** is set up with its own name, so passes meant for it can be recognized. It needs no key pair for this story, only Okta's public key.

**Step 1: The Report API gets a pass.**
When it needs prices, the Report API writes a short note: "I'm the Report API, asking for `read:billing`, sent now." It **signs** the note with its **private key** and sends it to Okta. Okta checks the signature with the Report API's **public key**, which it already has. Without the private key, no one can produce a valid signature, so no password is needed and no one else can get a pass.

Okta replies with an access token that expires in about an hour. Okta **signs** the token with its **private key**.

**Step 2: The Report API shows the pass to the Billing API.**
It asks for prices and attaches the token.

**Step 3: The Billing API checks the pass.**
It doesn't call Okta. It finds Okta's public key using the key ID in the token, and downloads it over HTTPS (the HTTPS certificate confirms the server really is Okta). Then it asks three questions:

1. **Is it genuine?** Does the signature check out with that public key? Any change to the token breaks it.
2. **Is it valid for me, right now?** Is the issuer Okta, is the audience the Billing API, and is the expiry in the future?
3. **Is it allowed to do this?** Does the token include `read:billing`?

If the first two fail, the answer is `401`: "I can't trust this pass." If the third fails, the answer is `403`: "I trust it, but it doesn't allow this." If all three pass, the Billing API returns the prices.

```
Setup:  Report API keeps private key; gives public key to Okta; gets client ID
        Okta keeps its signing private key; publishes its public key
Step 1: Report API signs a note with its private key ──> Okta checks with the public key
        Report API <── access token, signed by Okta's private key ── Okta
Step 2: Report API ──(token)──> Billing API
Step 3: Billing API finds Okta's public key by key ID, then checks:
          1. genuine? (signature)                          no → 401
          2. valid for me? (issuer, audience, expiry)      no → 401
          3. allowed? (scope includes read:billing)        no → 403
          all good → prices
```

### 29.B JWT: concept and example values

**What a JWT is.** A JWT (JSON Web Token) is the standard format of the access token. It's three parts separated by dots:

```
header.payload.signature
```

- **Header:** how the token was signed, and the key ID (`kid`) of the key used.
- **Payload:** the facts, called **claims**: who issued it, who it's for, when it expires, and what it allows.
- **Signature:** proof that Okta created the token and nobody changed it. It's made with Okta's private key.

The header and payload are encoded text that anyone can read. The signature is what makes them trustworthy.

**Header:**
```json
{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "kid": "2026-10-okta-key"
}
```
- `alg`: the signing method (RSA with SHA-256).
- `kid`: the label of the Okta key that signed it.

**Payload:**
```json
{
  "iss": "https://your-org.okta.com/oauth2/default",
  "aud": "api://billing",
  "sub": "0oa1rep2example",
  "cid": "0oa1rep2example",
  "scp": ["read:billing"],
  "iat": 1760000000,
  "exp": 1760003600
}
```
- `iss` (issuer): Okta issued it.
- `aud` (audience): meant for the Billing API.
- `sub` and `cid`: the Report API's client ID, since no person is involved.
- `scp` (scope): the allowed actions, here `read:billing`.
- `iat` (issued at) and `exp` (expires): Unix timestamps. This token lasts one hour.

**Signature:**
```
kR3x...long random-looking string...Qz9A
```
Okta calculates it from the header and payload, using its private key. Changing any character in the header or payload makes the check fail.

**How the Billing API uses each part:**
- The **signature** answers "Is it genuine?"
- The **payload** (`iss`, `aud`, `exp`) answers "Is it valid for me, right now?"
- The **payload** (`scp`) answers "Is it allowed to do this?"

### 29.C Interview version (about 60 seconds)

> "The Report API is a service, so it has its own identity in Okta. It proves itself with a private key, not a password: it signs a request and Okta checks it with the public key registered during setup. Okta returns an access token, a JWT, signed with Okta's private key. The token has three parts: a header with the key ID, a payload with issuer, audience, expiry and scope, and the signature. The Billing API finds Okta's public key by the key ID, checks the signature, then checks issuer, audience and expiry, then checks the scope. A bad signature or wrong audience or expiry gives 401, and a missing scope gives 403."

## 30. Spark Structured Streaming: Simple Explanation

**What this is:** a plain-language guide to Spark Structured Streaming, with a worked example. Use it to explain the idea first, then the details.

### 30.1 The idea

Structured Streaming treats a live stream of data as a table that keeps growing. New events are new rows added at the bottom. You write the same query you'd write for a batch job, and Spark keeps running it on new data as it arrives.

Three steps:

1. **The stream is a table.** New events are rows added to the bottom. Your query is a normal SQL-style query over that table.
2. **Spark runs it in small batches.** Every few seconds, it takes the new rows, runs your query on them, and updates the result. These small batches are called micro-batches.
3. **Spark remembers where it stopped.** A checkpoint records how far it got. If the job crashes, it restarts from that point instead of from the beginning.

### 30.2 The query

```python
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

events = spark.readStream.format("kafka") \
    .option("subscribe", "document-sourced") \
    .load()

counts = events.groupBy("sector").count()

counts.writeStream \
    .outputMode("complete") \
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/sector-counts") \
    .format("console") \
    .start()
```

Read it as: read from Kafka, count by sector, write the running totals, and checkpoint progress.

The example assumes each message has already been parsed so that `sector` is a column. In a real job, you first decode the message's JSON value, which Kafka delivers as raw bytes.

### 30.3 A worked example

**The incoming events**

```
Batch 1 (t = 0s):   USPF, CORP, USPF
Batch 2 (t = 5s):   GOV, USPF
Batch 3 (t = 10s):  CORP, CORP
```

**What Spark does with each batch:** it adds the new rows to the stream, reruns the count over everything seen so far, and writes the result. With `outputMode("complete")`, the whole table is written each time.

**Output after batch 1**

```
+------+-----+
|sector|count|
+------+-----+
|  USPF|    2|
|  CORP|    1|
+------+-----+
```

**Output after batch 2** (USPF goes from 2 to 3, and GOV appears)

```
+------+-----+
|sector|count|
+------+-----+
|  USPF|    3|
|  CORP|    1|
|   GOV|    1|
+------+-----+
```

**Output after batch 3** (CORP goes from 1 to 3)

```
+------+-----+
|sector|count|
+------+-----+
|  USPF|    3|
|  CORP|    3|
|   GOV|    1|
+------+-----+
```

**What to notice**

- Spark never restarts the count from zero. It updates the running totals with each batch.
- Each batch is a snapshot. If the job crashes after batch 2, the checkpoint lets it resume from there, so no event is counted twice.
- With `outputMode("update")`, each output would show only the sectors that changed in that batch, such as USPF and GOV after batch 2.

### 30.4 Three things to know

- **Output modes.** `append` writes only new rows. `update` writes only rows that changed. `complete` rewrites the whole result each time.
- **Late data and watermarks.** An event can arrive late. A watermark tells Spark how long to wait for late events before it closes a time window, so state doesn't grow forever.
- **Exactly-once.** With a checkpoint and a sink that handles retries (for example, idempotent writes), each event affects the result once, even after a crash.

### 30.5 Streaming vs batch

| | Batch | Structured Streaming |
|---|---|---|
| Input | A fixed set of data | Data that keeps arriving |
| Runs | Once, then stops | Continuously |
| Query code | Same | Same, plus stream options |
| Good for | Nightly loads | Near-real-time counts and alerts |

### 30.6 Where it fits in DCP

The platform's heavy batch work runs on Spark on Kubernetes. Structured Streaming suits live metrics, such as documents processed per sector per minute. The main document flow stays event-driven, with Kafka consumers in microservices, because each event needs its own transaction and business logic. See [§26.15](#2615-dcp-on-aws-the-full-footprint-native-vs-managed-spot-secrets-and-uploads) and [§18](#18-aws-likely-questions-and-dcp-mapped-concepts) for the Spark and Kafka footprint.

### 30.7 Interview version (about 30 seconds)

> "Structured Streaming treats the incoming stream as a table that keeps growing. I write the same query I'd write for batch, and Spark runs it in micro-batches, updating the result with each batch. A checkpoint records progress, so a restart resumes instead of double-counting. For late data I set a watermark, and for live metrics it's a good fit. For the core document flow I'd still use Kafka consumers, because each event needs its own transaction."

### 31.1 Types of Estimations

```text
Load estimation (QPS) - Predict the expected number of requests per second, data volume, or user traffic (DAU) for the system.
Storage estimation: Estimate the amount of storage required to handle the data generated by the system.
Bandwidth estimation: Determine the network bandwidth needed to support the expected traffic and data transfer.
Latency estimation: Predict the response time and latency of the system based on its architecture and components.
Resource estimation: Estimate the number of servers, CPUs, or memory required to handle the load and maintain desired performance levels.
~~~~~~
```

### 31.2 Key Characteristics of Distributed Systems

```text
Scalability - Increase #users/data/work w/o any impact to perf. Horizontal, Vertical (MySQL)
Reliability - continue working correctly in case of errors
Fault Tolerance - gracefully handle failures and continue operating, may be at reduced level
Availability - system should be up
Efficiency - do more with less resources
Serviceability or Manageability
Throughput (or bandwidth) - number of items delivered in a given time unit
```

### 31.3 Load Balancing

```text
We can add LBs at three places:
- Between the user and the web server
- Between web servers and an internal platform layer, like application servers or cache servers
- Between internal platform layer and database.

Redundant Load Balancers - Active, passive. Each LB monitors the health of the other and, since both of them are equally capable of serving traffic and failure detection, in the event the main load balancer fails, the second load balancer takes over.

Load Balancing Algorithms (trick to memorize?)
1. Round Robin
2. Least Connections
3. Weighted Round Robin
4. Weighted Least Connections
5. IP Hash
6. Least Response Time
7. Random
8. Least Bandwidth
9. Custom Load
~~~~~~
```

```text
The cache is a high-speed storage layer that sits between the application and the original source of the data, such as a database, a file system, or a remote web service.
Types of Caching
1. In-memory caching
2. Disk caching
3. Database caching
4. Client-side caching
5. Server-side caching
6. CDN caching
7. DNS caching
```

### 31.5 Data Partitioning

```text
Split a huge database into smaller independent chunks across multiple servers so each server handles its own data faster and in parallel.
Problem									=>	Solution
Too many rows, can't fit in one server" =>	Horizontal
Too many columns, accessing only a few" =>	Vertical
Both problems exist"					 => Hybrid

When to Use What
HORIZONTAL PARTITIONING
✓ Users growing rapidly (millions of users)
✓ Geographic distribution needed
✓ Load balancing critical
✗ Don't use if: Data access patterns differ wildly

VERTICAL PARTITIONING
✓ Some columns accessed way more than others
✓ Want to optimize cache/speed for hot data
✓ Storage optimization needed
✗ Don't use if: Need frequent joins across columns

HYBRID PARTITIONING
✓ Large-scale apps (Netflix, Uber, Amazon)
✓ Both scale AND optimization needed
✗ Don't use if: Team can't handle complexity
```
