### 32.6 My project: Kafka production issue and scalability story

- **Circuit breaker in extraction:** use retries for small transient failures, and open the circuit when failures continue.
- Pattern background: [MicroServices-Questions, pattern applicability in DCP](Java-And-MyProfessional-Projects-Interviews/MicroServices-Questions.md#pattern-applicability-in-dcp).

**Quick DCP decision guide**

| DCP situation | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Upload should return before extraction finishes | Kafka asynchronous messaging |
| SparkAir fails briefly | Timeout and retry with backoff |
| SparkAir keeps failing | Circuit breaker and Cognize fallback |
| Both AI providers fail | Manual extraction queue and user notification |
| One malformed document repeatedly fails | Dead-letter queue |
| The same Kafka event is delivered again | Idempotent consumer |
| Save document metadata and reliably publish an event | Transactional outbox |
| Simple automated sourcing-to-quality pipeline | Choreography |
| L1/L2 review with timers, escalation and rework | Orchestration |
| Publication fails after approval | Saga compensation and controlled retry |
| Reviewer dashboard needs a fast combined view | CQRS read model |
| Low-volume screen needs the freshest live status | API composition |
| Regulators need the complete document history | Event sourcing |
| Soniq becomes slow but extraction must continue | Bulkhead plus cache |
| One partner sends a very large traffic spike | Rate limiting |

**Summary answer:** "In microservices I avoid a distributed ACID transaction across service databases. I model the business transaction as a saga of local transactions. For a simple event pipeline I use choreography. For workflows with timeouts, branching or human approval I use orchestration. Each completed step has a compensating action, and every consumer is idempotent, because duplicate delivery is possible. I use event sourcing only where complete history, auditing or replay justify its complexity."

### 32.9 Java: OOPS concepts

- **Class:** a blueprint for creating objects. **Object:** an instance of a class.
- **Encapsulation:** protects data from direct access.
- **Abstraction:** hides unnecessary details.
- **Polymorphism:** the same method behaves differently for different types.
- **Inheritance:** reuses code from existing classes.

**Types of associations**

- **Aggregation (weak, "has-a"):** one class holds a reference to another, but both can exist independently. Example: a Company has Employees, and employees exist even if the company doesn't.
- **Composition (strong, "owns"):** the parent owns the child, and the child can't exist without it. Example: a House is composed of Rooms. If the house is destroyed, its rooms go too.

Full OOP notes: [OOPS.md](Java-And-MyProfessional-Projects-Interviews/OOPS.md) and [§22](#22-oops-object-oriented-design-reference).

### 32.10 Java: SOLID principles

| Principle | Rule | Practical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **S**ingle Responsibility | A class has one reason to change | Keep each class focused on one task |
| **O**pen/Closed | Open for extension, closed for modification | Add features with new code, without breaking old code |
| **L**iskov Substitution | Subclasses can replace their base class | Inheritance must not break correctness |
| **I**nterface Segregation | Clients don't depend on methods they don't use | Split fat interfaces into small ones |
| **D**ependency Inversion | Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes | Decouple high-level code from low-level details |

Detail and worked examples: [§22.1](#221-solid-principles).

- **Multithreading:** all synchronization techniques (`synchronized`, locks, atomic classes, volatile, latches, barriers).

### 32.12 Java: collections

**Core interfaces and when to use each**

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Random access and frequent end inserts | `ArrayList` |
| Frequent front or middle inserts and removes | `LinkedList` |
| Fast duplicate check and uniqueness | `HashSet` |
| Sorted and unique values | `TreeSet` |
| Insertion order and fast lookup | `LinkedHashSet` |
| Fast key to value lookup, any order | `HashMap` |
| Sorted key to value lookup | `TreeMap` |
| LRU cache (insertion order and fast lookup) | `LinkedHashMap` |
| Process by priority | `PriorityQueue` |
| Both ends matter (deque) | `ArrayDeque` |
| Undo and redo stack | `LinkedList` or `Deque` |
| Thread-safe map | `ConcurrentHashMap` |

**Operation costs (from the answer sheet)**

- **ArrayList:** `get(i)` is O(1). `add` at the end is O(1). Inserts, removes and searches in the middle or at the front are O(n), because elements shift.
- **LinkedList:** `add` and `remove` at the front or end are O(1). Access by index is O(n). Adding several items at the same position is cheap, because the iterator stays in place. Adding at random positions is O(n) each time, because the iterator must be repositioned.
- **HashSet and HashMap:** `contains` and `remove` by value are O(1) on average. They have no order.
- **TreeSet and TreeMap:** operations are O(log n), and results are sorted.
- 

**Characteristics**

| Collection | Ordered | Unique | Sorted | Duplicates | Random access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ArrayList | Yes | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| LinkedList | Yes | No | No | Yes | No |
| HashSet | No | Yes | No | No | No |
| TreeSet | No (sorted) | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| HashMap | No | Keys unique | No | Values only | No |
| TreeMap | No (sorted) | Keys unique | Yes | Values only | No |
| PriorityQueue | No | No | By priority | Yes | No |

**Real-world matches:** product list, ArrayList; email exists check, HashSet; leaderboard, TreeSet; urgent task queue, LinkedList; LRU cache, LinkedHashMap; user ID to profile, HashMap; process by priority, PriorityQueue; salary range search, TreeMap.

**Comparable and Comparator**

- **Comparable** defines the natural order inside the class, through `compareTo()`. A class can have only one natural order.
- **Comparator** defines custom sorting outside the class, so you can have several orders.

```java
class Movie implements Comparable<Movie> {
    String name; double rating; int year;
    Movie(String name, double rating, int year) {
        this.name = name; this.rating = rating; this.year = year;
    }
    public int compareTo(Movie other) {
        return this.year - other.year;          // natural order: by year
    }
}

// Custom orders, outside the class
Comparator<Movie> byRating = (a, b) -> Double.compare(b.rating, a.rating); // highest first
Comparator<Movie> byName   = (a, b) -> a.name.compareTo(b.name);

Collections.sort(movies);                       // uses compareTo (year)
Collections.sort(movies, byRating);             // uses the comparator
```

**hashCode() and equals()**

- If two objects are equal by `equals()`, they must return the same `hashCode()`.
- Override both together, using the same fields, or HashSet and HashMap will misbehave.
- This is the same bug as the `Trade` example in [Karat](#24-citi-karat-screening-round).

### 32.13 Java: String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer

- **String:** use when the value stays constant. It is immutable.
- **StringBuilder:** use when the value changes a lot and is used by one thread only. It is fast and not synchronized.
- **StringBuffer:** use when the value changes and several threads use it. It is synchronized, so it's thread-safe.
- Use StringBuilder when you don't need thread safety, since it's faster than StringBuffer.

## 33. Microservices: Interview Q&A

**What this is:** the microservices questions in one place, with a short answer for each and a link to the full material. The last part lists aspects that were missing from the earlier notes.

### 33.1 Why microservices are helpful

- **Independent deployment:** each service ships on its own schedule, so one team's release doesn't wait for everyone else.
- **Fault isolation:** a bug or a memory leak in one service doesn't take down the whole system. The blast radius is smaller.
- **Independent scaling:** scale only the hot service (for example, extraction workers) instead of the whole application.
- **Team ownership:** one team owns one service end to end, which speeds up decisions.
- **Technology choice per service:** each service can use the stack that fits its job.

💡 **MEMORY TRICK: "BLAST RADIUS"** (why a monolith is risky)

- **B**ottleneck: one team can't deploy its change without the whole app.
- **L**ocked together: teams wait on each other's releases.
- **A**ll-or-nothing: one failure takes everything down.
- **S**cales inefficiently: the whole app scales, even the part that is hot.
- **T**ech frozen: no part can move to a newer stack without moving everything.

Microservices shrink the blast radius: a failure stays inside one service.

**Full answer:** [§16](#16-microservices-when-pitfalls-culture-patterns). Use the DCP evidence: six services, extraction scaled 5 to 50 pods, and blast radius in [§26.3](#263-cut-production-incidents-60-and-mttr-6-by-re-architecting-legacy-monoliths-into-event-driven-microservices).

### 33.2 When microservices are not required

- **A small team or a simple product:** the overhead of many services, pipelines and deployments outweighs the benefit.
- **An unclear domain:** cutting services before the boundaries are known creates a distributed monolith.
- **Low scaling needs:** a modular monolith handles most loads well.
- **Strong data coupling:** if most features need the same tables in one transaction, splitting them adds cost and consistency problems.

**Rule of thumb:** start with a well-structured monolith, and extract a service when a clear boundary, scaling need or team boundary appears.

**Full answer:** [§16](#16-microservices-when-pitfalls-culture-patterns), including the "when is a modular monolith the right call" question.

### 33.3 Design patterns

- **Decomposition:** bounded contexts (DDD) and business capabilities.
- **Communication:** synchronous APIs for immediate answers; asynchronous messaging for everything else.
- **Data:** database per service, transactional outbox, idempotent consumers.
- **Transactions:** saga (orchestration or choreography) with compensating actions.
- **Resilience:** circuit breaker, bulkhead, timeouts, retries with backoff.
- **Edge:** API gateway, backend for frontend.

**Full answer:** [design patterns in summary](#microservice-design-patterns-in-summary-aligned-with-dcp), [golden rules](#golden-rules-of-microservices), and [Design Patterns](#design-patterns). DCP-specific mapping: [§26.1](#261-delivered-99-availability-and-95-accuracy-under-2s-latency-processing-10k-documentsday-dcp).

#### CQRS, explained simply

**The idea:** split the model that changes data (commands, the write side) from the model that reads it (queries, the read side). The name is Command Query Responsibility Segregation.

**Analogy:** a restaurant. The kitchen follows strict rules to prepare each order correctly. The menu board is built for quick reading by customers. Both are about the same food, but they are shaped for different jobs.

**Why:** writes need rules and consistency. Reads need speed and a shape that fits the screen. One model rarely does both well.

**Example in DCP:**
- **Write side (command):** an analyst approves a document. The approval rules run, PostgreSQL is updated, and a `DocumentApproved` event goes to the outbox and then to Kafka.
- **Read side (query):** the reviewer dashboard needs the document, its extraction, its approvals and its sector in one view. A projector listens to the events and builds a read model in MongoDB or Elasticsearch, shaped exactly for that screen. The dashboard reads from there, quickly, without joining five tables.

**Flow:** command → write model → event → projector → read model → query.

**The trade-off:**
- **Eventual consistency:** the dashboard may lag by seconds behind the write. Approval decisions should still read from the write side, the source of truth.
- **Two models to maintain:** more code and more moving parts.
- **Rebuildable:** if a read model breaks, you can rebuild it by replaying the events.

**When not to use it:** a small app where one model serves both reads and writes well. Don't add CQRS only because it sounds advanced.

**Relation to event sourcing:** CQRS and event sourcing are often used together, but they are separate ideas. CQRS splits reads from writes. Event sourcing stores events as the truth. You can use CQRS alone.

**Interview answer (about 30 seconds):** "CQRS separates the write model from the read model. In DCP, an approval updates the write side and publishes an event. A projector builds a read model shaped for the reviewer dashboard, so the screen loads fast. The cost is a few seconds of lag, so approval decisions still read from the source of truth."

⚠ *Confirm which read models DCP built (MongoDB, Elasticsearch, or both) before naming them.*

### 33.4 Security

- **Defense in depth (NAACS):** network, authentication, authorization, cryptography, secrets.
- **Identity:** OAuth 2.0 and OIDC for users; client-credentials tokens for service-to-service calls; mTLS inside the mesh.
- **Least privilege:** each service gets only the scopes and roles it needs.
- **Secrets and keys:** a secrets manager (Vault) for credentials, KMS for encryption, and no secrets in code or images.
- **Audit:** log every sensitive read and change.

**Full answer:** [Security in Microservices](#security-in-microservices), [§29](#29-oauth-20-and-jwt-service-to-api-story), and [§28 Q22](#28-wfs-senior-solution-architect-adp-qa).

### 33.5 Observability

- **Three signals (LMT):** logs (what happened), metrics (how it's performing), traces (where it's slow).
- **Correlation IDs** carried through HTTP and Kafka headers, so one request can be followed across services.
- **Tools:** Prometheus for metrics, Jaeger for traces, Splunk for logs, Grafana for dashboards.

**Full answer:** [Observability](#observability) and [How Jaeger, Splunk, Prometheus and Grafana connect](#how-jaeger-splunk-prometheus-and-grafana-connect).

### 33.6 Availability

- **No single point of failure:** replicas in several availability zones, and standby databases.
- **Asynchronous decoupling:** a slow dependency becomes lag, not an outage.
- **Each extra nine costs more:** 99.9% allows about 44 minutes of downtime a month. Multi-region failover is what 99.99% needs.

**Full answer:** [§26.16 How to reach 99%, 99.9% and 99.999% availability](#2616-how-to-reach-99-999-and-99999-availability).

### 33.7 Reliability

- **Retries with backoff and jitter**, only for transient errors and idempotent operations.
- **Idempotent consumers** and the transactional outbox, so duplicates and lost events don't corrupt data.
- **Circuit breakers and fallbacks**, so a failing service degrades gracefully.
- **Safe releases:** canary deployments with automatic rollback.

**Full answer:** [§27.10 retries without a retry storm](#2710-designing-retries-for-a-failing-downstream-without-a-retry-storm), [idempotent consumers and the outbox](#idempotent-consumers-vs-the-outbox-solving-double-processing), [blue-green and canary](#blue-green--canary-how-the-traffic-switch-actually-works).

#### Bulkhead, explained simply

**The idea:** a ship is built with walls (bulkheads) that split it into sealed compartments. If one compartment springs a leak, the water stays in that room, and the ship stays afloat.

**In software:** give each dependency or feature its own limited share of resources (threads, connections, or concurrent calls). If one slow dependency fills its share, the others keep working.

**Example in DCP:** the extraction service calls SparkAir (slow, external) and also serves approval requests from the database.
- **Without a bulkhead:** SparkAir slows down. Every request thread waits on it, all threads get stuck, and the approval screens stop working too. One slow vendor takes down the whole app.
- **With a bulkhead:** SparkAir gets its own pool, say 20 threads. When that pool is full, extra extraction calls fail fast or fall back to Cognize. The approval service has its own pool, so approvals keep working.

**Four common forms:**
- **Thread pool bulkhead:** a separate thread pool for each dependency.
- **Connection pool per dependency:** for example, a separate database pool for reporting, so reports can't use up the connections that approvals need.
- **Semaphore:** a cap on how many calls to one dependency run at the same time.
- **Per-tenant or per-sector limit:** one sector's burst can't use up another sector's share.

**How to size it:** pool size ≈ expected concurrent calls, plus some headroom. When a bulkhead is full, reject quickly rather than queue forever, so the caller can fall back or retry later.

**Works with the others:** the bulkhead limits how many calls run. A timeout stops a call that hangs. A circuit breaker stops calls once a dependency is clearly failing. Use all three together.

**In Java:** Resilience4j provides `@Bulkhead` (semaphore) and `ThreadPoolBulkhead`. Each Hikari connection pool is also a bulkhead for its database.

**Interview answer (about 30 seconds):** "A bulkhead gives each dependency its own limited pool of threads or connections, like watertight compartments on a ship. In DCP, if SparkAir slows down, only its pool fills up and fallback kicks in, while the approval service keeps its own threads. A bulkhead limits how much one dependency can take down, and a timeout and circuit breaker handle the rest."

⚠ *Check the pool sizes and the bulkhead names against DCP's configuration before quoting them.*

### 33.8 Scalability

- **Scale out, not up:** add instances behind a load balancer.
- **Partition the data** by key, so load spreads across servers.
- **Scale on the right signal:** queue lag and latency, not only CPU.
- **Remove the real bottleneck:** cache, batch, and fall back, as in the entity-mapping case.

**Full answer:** [§3 Distributed Systems](#3-distributed-systems--large-scale-compute-design) and [the entity-mapping bottleneck](#the-entity-mapping-bottleneck-explained-simply).

### 33.9 Other aspects worth covering

These were missing from the earlier notes. Each has a short answer.

- **API versioning and contracts:** version APIs, make only additive changes within a version, and use consumer-driven contract tests.
- **Testing across services:** contract tests for the boundaries, plus a small set of end-to-end tests. Don't rely on full-system tests for every change.
- **Data ownership:** each service owns its data. Other services use its API or events, never its tables.
- **Service discovery and configuration:** services find each other through a registry or the platform (Kubernetes DNS), and config comes from the environment or a config service.
- **Deployment and CI/CD:** each service has its own pipeline, and every change passes the same gates (tests, security scans, canary).
- **Debugging locally:** run the services you need with stubs for the rest, or use a shared dev environment.
- **Cost:** more services mean more infrastructure, monitoring and on-call. Count that cost before splitting.
- **Team topology:** service boundaries should match team boundaries ("business first"). See the BUSINESS FIRST trick in [§16](#16-microservices-when-pitfalls-culture-patterns).
- **Migration:** strangler fig, one capability at a time, with a numeric exit criterion for each step ([§16 roadmap](#roadmap-legacymonolith-to-microservices-wired-to-the-dcp-story)).
- **Kafka schema evolution:** a schema registry with compatibility rules ([Kafka questions](Java-And-MyProfessional-Projects-Interviews/Kafka-Questions.md)).

**Full answers in the earlier notes:** [§16 Other Microservices Questions](#16-microservices-when-pitfalls-culture-patterns).

**Interview date:** 2026-09-29
**Role:** Lead Java Engineer, XiP Compute Service (XCS) team — owns the most performance-critical component of Citi's unified risk-calculation platform (XiP/XiNG). Orchestrates 1.5B risk calculations/day across hundreds of thousands of pods and tens of thousands of compute nodes, private + public cloud. Parallelization regularly handles 250,000 compute-hours in a single 90-minute execution.

**Source material:** Answers below are grounded in the real DCP (Data Collection Platform) project write-ups in this repo — `Java-And-MyProfessional-Projects-Interviews/data-collection-platform/`, `Kafka-Questions.md`, `ARCHITECT_INTERVIEW_GUIDE.md`, `behavioral-mock.md` — plus GenAI project docs and the resume headline numbers. ## XiP/XiNG Platform — What It Actually Is (Public Info)

Verified via public reporting, not inferred from the JD — cross-checked across an industry trade article and two other live Citi job postings for the same XCS team at different levels (req 26975610 = this SVP role you're interviewing for; a parallel AVP req, 7+ yrs, identical platform language).

- **XiNG** ("Xi Next Generation," pronounced "zing") = Citi's standardized cross-asset quant library and risk/pricing engine. Started ~2014 in the fixed-income desk, built on an older internal analytics library ("Xi"), originally a post-2008-crisis regulatory response.
- **XiP** = the platform that runs XiNG at production scale — an API-services platform so the same valuation/risk data services are consumed consistently across business units, instead of each asset class building its own. **XCS ("XiP Compute Service") is the engine room inside XiP** — the compute orchestration layer specifically, which is exactly the team/role you're interviewing for.
- **Not just risk — "risk & suitability" calculations.** The actual job-posting language is "1.5 billion risk & suitability calculations," not risk alone. Suitability is a compliance/regulatory-fit concept (is this trade appropriate for this client), not just quantitative pricing risk — worth a clarifying question (§11).
- **Timeline**: ~6 years to expand from fixed income to credit, commodities, equities, risk/quant functions, equity mark-to-market accounting, and derivatives. By Q3 2024, "every trade at Citi goes through XiNG." CEO Jane Fraser cited it publicly on that quarter's earnings call as part of a broader simplification push (~1,250 legacy platforms retired since 2022).
- **Architecture**: Kubernetes-based orchestration, hybrid multi-cloud — on-prem core plus dynamic bursting to multiple public clouds, with placement decided by resource availability, latency, and cost. Self-service: quants can build custom pricing models (e.g. pricing callable bonds) with minimal code, without needing engineering for every new model. Some multi-hour calculations are threaded across many Kubernetes pods. Delivered ~10x improvement in calculation execution time as the platform matured.
- **Signal worth noting**: Citi is hiring across levels on this same XCS team concurrently (this SVP req + a parallel AVP req) — reads as active team growth, not a single backfill.
- **Led by** Jon Lofthouse (CIO since Feb 2025) working physically alongside Andy Morton (then head of rates trading, now head of Markets) — the reporting specifically credits physical proximity between tech and trading-desk leadership as pivotal to how it got built.

Sources: [XiNG: Inside Citi's all-encompassing risk platform (WatersTechnology)](https://www.waterstechnology.com/data-management/7952400/xing-inside-citis-all-encompassing-risk-platform) · [Derivatives house of the year: Citi (Risk.net)](https://www.risk.net/awards/7962588/derivatives-house-of-the-year-citi) · [AVP req, same team](https://jobs.citi.com/job/pune/java-developer-distributed-systems-assistant-vice-president/287/99709913104)
